1. Case Study Overview

This report presents the Phase 1 deliverable for Group 07 of the Continuous Assessment Exam: a Resilient Distributed

DAG Orchestrator. The system implements a directed-acyclic-graph (DAG) task execution abstraction on top of raw

cloud primitives -- specifically a managed cloud queue (SQS/Pub-Sub style) and an elastically scaling compute fleet --

and layers on top of them a custom state-machine engine that tracks the lifecycle of every DAG and every task within

it, with deterministic replay through checkpointing so that no in-flight work is silently lost on failure.

Group ID 07

Case Study Title Resilient Distributed DAG Orchestrator

Underlying Cloud Primitives

Cloud Queue (Amazon SQS / Google Cloud Pub/Sub), Compute Auto-Scaling Groups

State-machine DAG execution engine with deterministic replay checkpointing

System Design Layer Built On Top

Guarantees Targeted Fault tolerance (crash recovery of both workers and the control plane), at-least- once task execution with idempotent replay, and linearizable reads of DAG execution state

1.1 Problem Motivation

Raw cloud queues and auto-scaling compute groups give delivery and elasticity, but neither understands task

dependencies, ordering, or partial-failure semantics. A naive pipeline that fires tasks onto a queue has no way to know

when a downstream task is safe to start, cannot resume correctly after a crash mid-DAG, and offers no consistent view

of “where the workflow currently stands.” The abstraction layer built here closes that gap: it turns a set of unordered,

independently-retryable queue messages into a coherent, resumable, dependency-aware workflow engine.

1.2 Design Scope for Phase 1

• A System Architecture Diagram showing how the custom orchestration layer sits above the raw cloud primitives

(Section 2).

• A Data & Control Pathway specification mapping client read/write paths, background worker tasks, and network

boundaries (Section 3).

• A Failure & Edge Case Strategy identifying component crash behavior, network partition handling, and data

recovery steps (Section 4).

2. System Architecture Diagram

The diagram below shows the full structural layout of the system. Components are color-coded by role: control plane

(blue), data plane / workers (green), raw cloud primitives that the abstraction is built on top of (brown), durable storage

(purple), and the external client (grey). The dashed red boundary marks the cloud VPC -- everything inside it has no

direct public ingress except through the API Gateway.

Figure 1: System architecture -- custom DAG state-machine layer over raw cloud primitives

2.1 Component Responsibilities

Orchestrator Control Plane -- the heart of the abstraction layer. It holds the DAG state machine: for every submitted DAG it tracks which nodes are PENDING, READY, RUNNING, SUCCEEDED, FAILED, or DEAD-LETTERED, and decides which tasks become schedulable as their dependencies resolve. It is the only component permitted to enqueue new work onto the Task Queue.

Metadata / State Store -- a durable, strongly-consistent store holding DAG definitions, per-task status, and a monotonically-versioned execution state. All reads of “current DAG status” are served from here so that concurrent readers see a linearizable view.

Write-Ahead Log (WAL) -- an append-only, durable log of every state transition the control plane makes. This is what makes replay deterministic: replaying the WAL from the last checkpoint reconstructs the exact same in-memory state machine, regardless of which physical control-plane replica performs the replay.

Task Queue (raw primitive: SQS / Pub-Sub) -- the raw, at-least-once delivery primitive. The orchestration layer never trusts it for ordering or exactly-once semantics; it only relies on it for durable, elastic fan-out of ready work to workers.

View original page — includes the original diagrams, flowcharts and layout
SOURCE PAGE 4 / 10

Worker Pool (raw primitive: Compute Auto-Scaling Group) -- a fleet of stateless task executors that scales horizontally with queue depth. Workers hold no DAG knowledge -- they only know how to execute one task, checkpoint its output, and report completion or failure.

Checkpoint Store -- durable object storage holding task outputs and periodic execution snapshots, so that recovery never has to re-derive results that were already produced.

Completion Event Queue -- the feedback channel that lets the control plane learn about task outcomes asynchronously and advance the DAG state machine accordingly.

Dead-Letter Queue -- the terminal sink for tasks that exhaust their retry budget, isolating poison messages from healthy traffic.

Health Monitor -- a background loop that tracks worker heartbeats and lease timeouts, independently of the main control plane request path, so that a stalled or crashed worker's task can be reclaimed even if the worker never reports failure itself.

3. Data & Control Pathways

This section maps the concrete paths that data and control signals take through the system: the client write path

(submitting a DAG), the client read path (polling status), and the background worker path (task execution,

checkpointing, and event feedback) -- along with the network boundary each path crosses.

Figure 2: Client read/write paths and background worker pathway, with network boundaries

3.1 Client Write Path (Submitting a DAG)

• 1. The client issues an authenticated POST /dag request over TLS to the API Gateway -- this is the only write entry

point exposed to the public network.

• 2. The gateway validates the DAG specification (schema, cycle-detection, permissions) and forwards a validated

job to the Orchestrator Control Plane.

• 3. The control plane persists the DAG graph and initial per-task states to the Metadata Store (3a) and, in the

same logical transaction, appends the corresponding entries to the WAL and enqueues every task with no unmet dependencies onto the Task Queue as immediately schedulable work (3b).

3.2 Client Read Path (Status Queries)

Status reads never touch the queue or the workers directly -- they are served from the Metadata / State Store through

the control plane, which guarantees the client always observes a linearizable, monotonically-advancing view of DAG

View original page — includes the original diagrams, flowcharts and layout
SOURCE PAGE 6 / 10

progress rather than a possibly-stale or reordered one. This path is entirely read-only and idempotent, so it is safe to

poll aggressively or expose as a webhook callback.

3.3 Background Worker Path

• 5. A worker in the Auto-Scaling Group dequeues a ready task from the Task Queue.

• 6. On completion, the worker writes its output/checkpoint to the Checkpoint Store before acknowledging

anything else -- output durability is established before the event is announced.

• 7. The worker publishes a success or failure event to the Completion Event Queue.

• 8. The control plane consumes that event, advances the DAG state machine, and -- if the completed task

unblocks other nodes -- enqueues the newly-ready downstream tasks, closing the loop back into the write path.

Running alongside this, the Health Monitor independently tracks heartbeats and lease renewals between itself and the

Worker Pool, and reports dead workers straight to the control plane so that an orphaned task can be reclaimed and

rescheduled without any client involvement.

3.4 Network Boundaries

• Public boundary: only the API Gateway is internet-facing; it terminates TLS and is the sole ingress into the

system.

• Private subnet: the Orchestrator Control Plane, Task Queue, WAL, Worker Pool, Checkpoint Store, Completion

Event Queue, and Health Monitor all live inside the VPC with no public ingress -- workers only make outbound calls to the queue and storage endpoints.

• Egress control: workers and the control plane reach the Metadata Store and Checkpoint Store over private VPC

endpoints, avoiding any traversal of the public internet for internal data-plane traffic.

4. Failure & Edge Case Strategy

Every task in the system moves through an explicit state machine, shown below, so that failure handling is never ad hoc

-- each transition (retry, dead-letter, or replay-based recovery) is a defined edge in the same graph that governs normal

execution.

Figure 3: Per-task state machine, including retry, dead-letter, and WAL-replay recovery transitions

4.1 Component Crash Behavior

Worker crash -- detected purely through the absence of heartbeats/lease renewal at the Health Monitor rather than any self-reported signal, since a crashed worker cannot report anything. Its in-flight task's lease is allowed to expire and the task is returned to READY for another worker to claim. Because task handlers are written to be idempotent (keyed by a task-attempt ID), a task that was actually finished just before the crash but never acknowledged can safely re- execute without corrupting state.

Orchestrator (control plane) crash -- the control plane is deployed as a replicated set with leader election. On leader loss, a standby replica is promoted and rebuilds its entire in-memory DAG state machine by replaying the Write-Ahead Log forward from the last durable checkpoint in the Metadata Store. Because every state transition was appended to the WAL before it was considered committed, replay is deterministic: the recovered state is bit-for-bit equivalent to the state immediately before the crash.

Queue / broker unavailability -- since the Task Queue and Completion Event Queue are managed cloud primitives (SQS/Pub-Sub), the orchestrator treats transient unavailability as a retryable condition with backoff rather than a fatal error, buffering scheduling decisions in the Metadata Store until publishing succeeds.

4.2 Network Partition Handling

If the control plane and a subset of workers become partitioned from each other, workers do not block: they continue

executing whatever task they already dequeued, since the task payload and execution logic do not require an active

View original page — includes the original diagrams, flowcharts and layout
SOURCE PAGE 8 / 10

connection to the control plane. What they cannot do during a partition is report completion or receive new work, so

their queue visibility timeout will eventually expire. On reconnection, the system reconciles state against the Metadata

Store and Task Queue -- which remain the durable sources of truth -- rather than trusting any node's local view formed

during the partition. This makes the design partition-tolerant in the CAP sense: it favors availability of task execution

during a partition, while relying on idempotency and version-checked writes to the Metadata Store to preserve

correctness once the partition heals, rather than blocking all progress until connectivity is restored.

A partition between the control plane and the Metadata Store itself is treated more conservatively: rather than risk

scheduling on stale or unknown state, the control plane pauses new scheduling decisions and serves reads with an

explicit staleness flag until the store is reachable again -- the system fails closed on its own source of truth, while still

failing open on worker connectivity.

4.3 Data Recovery Steps

• Step 1 -- Detect: leader-election liveness probes (control plane) and heartbeat/lease expiry (workers) identify the

failed component.

• Step 2 -- Isolate: the failed component's in-flight work is not trusted; its task leases are revoked or its leadership

token is invalidated so no split-brain writes occur.

• Step 3 -- Replay: a fresh control-plane replica (or, for a worker, simply a fresh worker) reconstructs required state

-- from the WAL and last checkpoint for the control plane, or by re-fetching the task definition and its idempotency key for a worker.

• Step 4 -- Resume: recovered/rescheduled tasks re-enter the state machine at READY (or RETRYING, if this is a

repeat failure), and normal scheduling continues from exactly that point -- no DAG has to be restarted from the beginning.

• Step 5 -- Reconcile duplicates: any task result produced twice because of at-least-once delivery is deduplicated

using the idempotency key recorded in the Metadata Store before the result is allowed to affect downstream scheduling.

4.4 Edge Cases

Failure Scenario Detection Mechanism System Response Data Impact

Worker crash mid-task Missed heartbeat / lease expiry at the Health Monitor (configurable lease TTL, e.g. 30s)

Task lease is revoked; task is moved back to READY and re- enqueued onto the Task Queue for another worker to pick up

No loss -- task re-executes; idempotency keys prevent duplicate side effects

Task fails (exception / non-zero exit)

Worker reports explicit failure event on the Completion Event Queue

State machine transitions task to RETRYING with exponential backoff; after N attempts, task moves to FAILED and then DEAD-LETTERED

Failure captured in WAL; task payload preserved in Dead-Letter Queue for manual inspection

Orchestrator (control plane) crash

Loss of leader lease in the coordination service / failed liveness probe

A standby control-plane replica is promoted; it rebuilds in- memory DAG state by replaying the Write-Ahead Log from the last durable checkpoint

Zero state loss - - WAL guarantees the rebuilt state is identical to pre- crash state (deterministic replay)

Network partition between control plane and workers

Queue visibility timeout expiry and heartbeat gaps observed asymmetrically on each side

Workers continue executing in- flight tasks (partition-tolerant); on reconnection, both sides reconcile against the queue and metadata store, which act as the source of truth

Duplicate execution is possible during partition -- mitigated by idempotent task handlers and version- checked writes

Duplicate task delivery (at-least-once queue semantics)

Idempotency key already present in the Metadata Store for that task attempt

Duplicate execution is detected and the redundant result is discarded before it can double- apply side effects

No corruption -- exactly-once effect is achieved on top of at-least-once delivery

Metadata / State Store unavailable

Write/read timeout on state-store client calls

Control plane pauses issuing new scheduling decisions and serves cached reads (with a staleness flag) until the store recovers; no destructive action is taken blind

No loss -- system fails closed rather than proceeding on unknown state

Poison task (task that always fails)

Retry counter reaches the configured maximum

Task is moved to the Dead- Letter Queue instead of retrying indefinitely; downstream DAG nodes dependent on it are marked BLOCKED, not silently skipped

Preserves DAG correctness -- no downstream node executes on missing/failed input

5. Summary

The Resilient Distributed DAG Orchestrator demonstrates how a thin but carefully-designed abstraction layer -- a state-

machine execution engine backed by a write-ahead log -- can convert a raw, best-effort cloud queue and an elastic but

stateless compute fleet into a workflow platform with strong guarantees: deterministic crash recovery, partition

tolerance without blocking worker progress, and idempotent, exactly-once task effects on top of at-least-once delivery.

Phase 1 has established the structural architecture, the concrete data and control pathways with their network

boundaries, and an explicit per-task state machine covering every failure and recovery transition the system needs to

handle. Phase 2 will implement this design in code, together with fault-injection tests that exercise each of the scenarios

identified in Section 4.4 and benchmark the orchestrator's throughput and recovery-time characteristics under load.
